newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany offers pioneering bill to police the Internet.
newsitem.headline: Germany offers pioneering bill to police the Internet.

text.p: Just days after prosecutors indicted a CompuServe executive on pornography charges, the German government introduced pioneering legislation Friday to police the Internet.

Introduction of the Information and Communications Services Bill came just days after state prosecutors announced the surprise indictment of the local head of CompuServe Corp. for allegedly aiding in the dissemination of pornography on the Internet in Germany.

"The Internet must not become a legal vacuum. This country is not prepared to tolerate certain things that appear there," Technology Minister Juergen Ruettgers said in defending the government's proposed tough laws to fight illegal misuse of the global computer network.

He specifically defended Germany's efforts to stop neo-Nazi electronic magazines on the World Wide Web, usually located abroad but accessable by Germans over the Internet, from distributing diatribes that deny the Nazis killed Jews in concentration camp gas chambers, the so-called "Auschwitz Lie," which is illegal here.
"We must continue to forbid the Auschwitz lie, regardless of whether it is spread in black and white or in bit and byte," Ruettgers told the sparsely-attended debate.
Bonn has also stepped up efforts to fight pornographic images, easily seen by children on Web sites around the world. Certain hard-core images are illegal in Germany.

Bavarian prosecutors this week indicted Felix Somm, the head of CompuServe's German and central European operations, on charges of aiding the exchange of child pornography and extremist propaganda via its online service.
Ruettgers said, however, that the issue of online smut should not be blown out of proportion.

"We are talking here about just 1 percent of the total content available on the Internet, so I don't want discussion of these things to get the upper hand," he said. "But it is still important that we have some rules and guidelines."

While the proposed law would set standards for child protection in cyberspace, it mainly seeks to define which activities require regulation and which can be operated without any formal license or regulatory oversight.

To do this it distinguishes between traditional media forms that use the Internet, and should therefore fall under media regulations, and new services, such as electronic mail, that the government says should not be classified as media.
"It is important that this law has come," said Ruettgers. "We are the first country in the world that has launched an effort to clearly define the legal framework (for multimedia services)."

Speaking for the opposition Social Democrats, deputy chairman Wolfgang Thierse said trying to censor the Internet would fail, but he called for the police to set up a national coordination centre to monitor illegal online activities.

While censorship of Internet providers is commonplace in countries such as China and Singapore, Germany appears to be the first Western democracy to indict an official of an online service for Internet content considered illegal.
The move by prosecutors in the state of Bavaria Wednesday marked a decisive turning point in the debate over Internet regulation by government authorities.
More criminal charges against online service providers are expected in Germany following the indictment of the head of a unit of CompuServe, lawyers and industry experts said.

"There is hardly an online service or Internet service provider in Germany today that has not been the subject of a criminal investigation," said Michael Schneider, an attorney who specialises in computer law.

In the case of CompuServe, prosecutors indicted Felix Somm, head of its German and Central European operations, for allegedly aiding in the trafficking of child pornography and the dissemination of Nazi symbols and violent computer games that are illegal in Germany.
CompuServe, a unit of H&R Block Inc., based in Columbus, Ohio, said it considered the charges against Somm to be baseless and expected him to be acquitted.
